subject: Automotive & EVs
title: How Brakes Work
description: A quick, practical guide to How Brakes Work.

hook.text: Stopping a two-ton car from 60 mph in seconds requires converting motion into heat—lots of heat.

buildup.text: When you press the brake pedal, hydraulic fluid pushes pads against spinning metal discs called rotors.

discovery.text: Friction between pads and rotors converts kinetic energy into thermal energy. The car slows down.

twist.text: Brake rotors can reach 1,000°F during hard stops. That's why track cars have brake cooling ducts.

climax.text: If brakes overheat, they 'fade'—the pedal feels soft and stopping distance grows dangerously.

punchline.text: Brakes are just heat machines that trade speed for warmth.

details.summary: When you press the brake pedal, hydraulic fluid transmits force to calipers that squeeze friction pads against spinning rotors, converting the car's kinetic energy into heat to slow it down.
details.whyItMatters: Brakes are the single most critical safety system on any vehicle. Understanding how they work helps drivers recognize warning signs and maintain them properly.
takeaways: Hydraulic pressure multiplies the force from your foot
Disc brakes use calipers and pads squeezing a spinning rotor
Brake fade occurs when overheated components lose friction

faq.question: How often should brake pads be replaced?
faq.answer: Typically between 25,000 and 70,000 miles depending on driving style, vehicle weight, and pad material. Squealing or grinding sounds and longer stopping distances are warning signs of worn pads.

faq.question: Why do brakes sometimes feel spongy?
faq.answer: Air bubbles in the hydraulic fluid compress under pressure, reducing braking force and creating a spongy feel. Bleeding the brake lines to remove air restores firm pedal response.
